paras: The killing of Andy Hightower was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a deputy sheriff and a second man at Rome, Georgia, on the afternoon of August 3, 1895. Hightower, said to be wanted on warrants elsewhere, died the next morning after physicians had expected him to recover, and a coroner's jury was convened.

According to a Rome dispatch to the Savannah Morning News, Hightower was "wanted in Cedartown and other places" when officers tried to arrest him. A later dispatch, attributing the claims to hearsay ("it is said"), added that he faced several warrants at Cedartown and was wanted for killing a man at Talladega, Alabama.

Deputy Sheriff J. K. Williamson and Raymond McConnell fired at Hightower when, by their account, he resisted arrest and tried to escape. He kept running and reached a swamp, but finding that a bullet had struck him and believing he would die, he came back and surrendered. Physicians judged the wound "not necessarily fatal," and the first report said he was expected to recover.

Instead, Hightower died at 10 o'clock on the morning of August 4. Thirty minutes earlier, the dispatch said, one of the attending physicians had left him saying he would soon be able to resume work "at the furnace."

A coroner's jury was organized on August 4 but adjourned until the next day to hear more witnesses. No report of the jury's verdict, or of any charge against Williamson or McConnell, was found in the coverage.

The shooting is known from two short Rome dispatches printed in the Savannah Morning News on August 4 and August 5. The first ran under the headline "FLED UNDER FIRE" and told the officers' version as fact, describing "A Negro Shot in Trying to Escape From an Officer of the Law." The second, headed "HIGHTOWER GONE HIGHER" with the subhead "His Bad Name," reported the death alongside unproven warrants and closed with the line "He bore a bad character."
No Black-press account of the shooting was found, and no other paper's report turned up, so the officers' description of resistance and flight stands without a second version.

accounts.label: Officers' account (Rome dispatch)
accounts.gist: Hightower resisted arrest and tried to escape; both men fired, he ran into a swamp, and on finding himself wounded he returned and gave himself up.

accounts.label: Rome dispatch, next day
accounts.gist: He died the next morning, shortly after a physician said he would soon be back at work; the dispatch added hearsay that he was wanted on several warrants and for a killing in Alabama.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News ran the officers' version as fact under 'FLED UNDER FIRE' and followed with 'HIGHTOWER GONE HIGHER ... His Bad Name', listing unproven warrants and calling him a man who 'bore a bad character'.
